paper.title: Accurate prediction of tensorial spectra using equivariant graph neural network
paper.research_summary: Here we introduce the Tensorial Spectra Equivariant Neural Network (TSENN), an equivariant graph neural network architecture that maps crystal structures directly to their full photon-frequency-dependent optical tensors. By encoding isotropic sequential scalar components and anisotropic sequential tensor components into spherical tensor representations, TSENN ensures symmetry-aware predictions consistent with crystalline symmetry constraints. Trained on frequency-dependent dielectric tensors of 1,432 bulk semiconductors, the model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.127, demonstrating its potential for efficient and general modeling of optical properties.

task.objective: map crystal structures directly to their full photon-frequency-dependent optical tensors
constraints: symmetry-aware predictions consistent with crystalline symmetry constraints

evidence.text: Here we introduce the Tensorial Spectra Equivariant Neural Network (TSENN), an equivariant graph neural network architecture that maps crystal structures directly to their full photon-frequency-dependent optical tensors.

stages.stage_name_raw: dataset selection and ab initio calculation
stages.stage_goal: acquire frequency-dependent dielectric tensors for 1432 bulk semiconductors via first-principles methods
stage_input: structural constraints (fewer than three elements, fewer than ten atoms per unit cell)

evidence.text: With our focus on small bandgap semiconductors in mind, we selected materials from the Materials Project41 with bandgaps ranging from 0.3 to 3 eV (photon wavelengths of 4100 nm (infrared) to 413 nm (violet)) that are appropriate for optoelectronic applications42,43. To maintain structural stability, we imposed an energy-above-hull threshold of 0.02 eV/atom. For computational efficiency, we limited our selection to materials with fewer than three elements and fewer than ten atoms per unit cell. Additionally, we excluded magnetic materials as well as materials containing elements with f electrons due to the lack of availability of accurate, predefined pseudo-potential sets. These constraints yielded a dataset of 1432 materials...
By training TSENN on the aforementioned dataset, we achieve a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.127 in the predicted imaginary part of the dielectric tensor.
DFT calculations were performed using OpenMX37–40... The dielectric tensor was computed within the IPA using the Kubo formula...

stages.stage_goal: transform Cartesian dielectric tensors into spherical-harmonics basis to encode rotational symmetry

evidence.text: To predict the dielectric tensor using an equivariant neural network, we express it in the spherical-harmonics basis, which naturally encodes rotational symmetry. The dielectric tensor is symmetric under the permutation of Cartesian indices, εij = εji, and therefore admits the decomposition εij = Tαβ Y α 1 Y β 1 = ε(0)  ε(2) = Σ‘∈{0, 2} Σ‘ m = −‘ εm (‘) Y m ‘ , (1) which separates the scalar trace component (ℓ= 0) from the traceless symmetric tensor component (ℓ= 2).
This approach transforms the tensors from the Cartesian basis into the spherical-harmonics basis, making it easier to work with tensor properties in systems with rotational and inversion symmetries.

stages.stage_name_raw: training TSENN with composite loss function
stages.stage_goal: train equivariant graph neural network to predict ℓ=0 and ℓ=2 spherical-harmonic components from crystal graphs

evidence.text: After the final pointwise convolution layer, we apply mean pooling over all nodes to obtain a global representation of the material. The network output is then partitioned into two parts: a scalar component corresponding to ℓ= 0 and a tensor component corresponding to ℓ= 2.
To train the model, we define a composite loss function L, which separately evaluates the scalar and tensor components of the predicted optical spectra.

stages.stage_name_raw: evaluation using MAE and symmetry-preserving metrics
stages.stage_goal: evaluate model performance using MAE, anisotropy errors, and symmetry validation

evidence.text: To evaluate the model’s performance, the most direct measure is the MAE of the dielectric tensor, MAE = 1/(6nω) Σω Σα≤β |bεαβ(ω) − εαβ(ω)|.

The overall tensor MAE is 0.127 (0.097 median), establishing TSENN’s robust baseline accuracy. When decomposed into isotropic and anisotropic contributions, the averaged anisotropic error MAEaniso is 0.096 (0.074 median), demonstrating reliable capture of directional variations.
To further confirm symmetry preservation, we applied a symmetry-based masking procedure to the predicted tensor at each photon energy (see Methods).

stages.stage_name_raw: Kramers–Kronig reconstruction and strain-based symmetry breaking tests
stages.stage_goal: validate physical consistency by reconstructing real parts via K–K relations and testing response to symmetry-breaking strain

evidence.text: With the accurately predicted imaginary parts, we used K–K relations to obtain the real parts of the dielectric tensors. Since K–K relations are model-independent, they provide a rigorous test of the internal consistency of the predicted spectra.

We also evaluated the model’s response to shear strain perturbations by modifying the lattice angles... As the angular deviation increases, a finite bεxz(ω) progressively emerges, producing a nonzero |bεxz|. We quantified this emergent behavior as a function of the shear angle and observed an almost perfect linear relationship in the small-strain regime (R² = 0.995).
